abstract: Oral administration is convenient, noninvasive, and highly acceptable to patients, yet many polar, hydrophilic, and macromolecular therapeutics remain difficult to deliver efficiently because of poor transport across the intestinal epithelium. Inspired by mosquitoes, which use small-amplitude vibration to reduce tissue resistance during proboscis insertion, we hypothesize that localized, gentle mechanical vibration could provide a gentle and controllable physical strategy to enhance intestinal drug absorption. Here, using an ex vivo intestinal absorption evaluation system, we show that mechanical vibration regulates drug transport in a molecule-dependent manner, selectively enhancing the absorption of strongly polar and hydrophilic drugs and biological macromolecules while reducing tissue transport of drugs with relatively high intrinsic permeability. We further develop a soft oral pill (SOP) that combines magnetic guidance, mucosal adhesion, localized drug release, and externally programmable vibration to promote mechanically assisted transepithelial transport. In diabetic rabbits, vibration-assisted delivery with the SOP achieves a relative oral bioavailability of ∼16% for insulin, ∼16-fold higher than oral insulin administration alone, and induces sustained glucose lowering. This work establishes vibration-assisted mucosal delivery as a minimally invasive and remotely controllable strategy for expanding the oral delivery of poorly absorbed therapeutics.
